[Ryan Walker] may have written up his observations a few years ago, but the lessons are just as relevant today as they were back then. He shares five easy ways to sink your hardware startup. It’s a reminder that while hardware startups are unique, there are basic business realities that still apply because the hardware itself is going to be only one part of a whole. These business fundamentals can be a drag, but it’s worth giving them some attention. But if that’s not your jam, no worries. As [Ryan] experienced, they will explain themselves one way or another. A good one is skipping market research. Do customers actually exist for this thing? Or forgoing market testing — do the customers actually want it enough to pay for it? One of the worst things to be stuck with is a product that everyone likes, but nobody wants to buy. Premature optimization is another good one that a number of our readers can probably relate to in one way or another. It’s one thing to buy a tool or a part that one doesn’t end up needing, but when that gets scaled up it can put a real dent in a fledgling business’s development. We’ve also shared insights on what it takes to develop a product and get it out there, whether as a solo entrepreneur or as part of a larger team, to help nudge the process toward success. One of those missing words the eyes just slide right off of… Relevant with Naya B.V. just going bankrupt and leaving nata create owners (and people who prepaid for float, also me, oof never doing that again) in the lurch “startup” causes a cringe so deep that my skin unzips and my skeleton leaves my body. Call your business a startup is a 100 percent chance that I will not look at what your product even is. Also the last thing we need on this planet is more product. Services then? Anyone who wants to have a hardware startup should read “The Four Hour Workweek” by Timothy Ferriss. He explains a lot of techniques for starting and running a small “hardware” business that’s temporary in nature, techniques that are directly applicable to the “hardware” that people are thinking about on this site. From the book: Market research can be done with a couple of web pages and some google ad words. Put up a description of your product, have a purchase page, and when people go to enter their credit card/paypal information, have a page that says “this product is currently on backorder, if you like you can leave your E-mail and we’ll send you a notice when it becomes available”. (Of note: This is legal so long as you don’t actually take the credit card number.) This gives you a good sense of how many people would actually purchase the product, which is precisely the information you need when starting a business. He also goes through resources that can make your business life much easier; for example, once you have the actual product you can outsource the warehousing, boxing, and shipping to another company. Of course this reduces your profit, but it also reduces your workload. A number of these resources exist for outsourced functions, such as billing/payment, customer service, and so on. The book goes through one case study where a student on holiday in France saw some french sailor shirts that aren’t available in the US and she thought these would sell. She did the market research, had the producer in France ship shirts to the warehouse in lots of 300, had several rounds of this, noted that the big players started copying the design, and closed the business. Several months and a tidy profit. Other than the hardware being different (and self designed by you), this model is exactly what a short-run hardware business should use. Optimization is best left to future you, and this applies to the business as well. Once your product is selling well and the business is running smoothly, that’s the time to decide whether warehousing and shipping is better done in-house. And of course, the general rule applies: if you want to start a business, research how to do that. It’s not difficult, but there are a lot of pitfalls that can ruin the experience. I’m surprised at how few people are familiar with this book and Tim’s overall work. How books and podcast are a gold mine of dense real world information that most people on the planet just will never have access to without him. That’s such a good book for just getting familiar with the process and building confidence. Found it in 2013 and have VERY slowly been working up the skills and confidence start my own little business. Hardest part has been figuring out what I am passionate enough about to actually stick with it. Still working on that. That book is still good stuff to this day. Thanks for sharing. The company says Archy is over 90% accurate and will be part of an AI system rolling out from 2027. Archy has been more than 90% accurate in early tests, McDonald’s said, according to Restaurant Dive. The company has not said how many restaurants use it, but Fox News reported in June that it was being tested at five US locations. Archy is one part of ArchIQ, a generative AI system for running restaurants. It also tracks stock, watches kitchen equipment with cameras and uses scales to check that orders are complete before they reach customers, Restaurant Dive reported. McDonald’s said the drive-thru tools can save each restaurant more than 50 hours of staff time a week. It also said ArchIQ can cut food waste by 15%. The system runs on Google Cloud edge computers, which process data inside the restaurant. They are already installed in thousands of McDonald’s locations, and the company expects to finish the US edge rollout in 2027. “This allows our AI models to make accurate split-second decisions,” said Brian Rice, McDonald’s global chief information officer. McDonald’s has tried AI ordering before. It ended a drive-thru test with IBM in June 2024. Meanwhile, rivals have moved ahead, and Taco Bell now uses voice AI ordering at more than 890 US restaurants. ArchIQ is part of the company’s wider Next strategy. McDonald’s plans about $8.5bn in franchisee support through 2036, covering rent relief and restaurant investment, according to its investor day release. The company will roll out ArchIQ tools in stages starting in 2027. It has not given a date for a full Archy launch. Armed FantasiaJRPGKickstarterPenny BloodWild Arms  In 2022, a new supergroup of JRPG veterans called WILD BUNCH Productions launched a dual Kickstarter to create successors for two dormant series. Armed Fantasia, a fantasy western in the vein of Wild Arms, and the gothic Penny Blood, following up on Shadow Hearts. Despite successfully crowdfunding more than two million dollars at the time, resources stretched thin quickly, prompting the team to seek out a publisher. Now it seems like it’s the end of the road for Armed Fantasia, as a financial statement suggests the game has been “discontinued.” As spotted by Automaton Media, an investor document from 505 Games parent company Digital Bros confirms that they were the silent partner for Armed Fantasia. It also confirms that they arenât anymore. The statement suggests that the game has ceased development, and that “the decisions followed a thorough review of the potential of each product in consideration of changing market conditions and the additional investment required.” While signs of life on both games have been sporadic, a post from producer Akifumi Kaneko last March confirmed the team had sent a build to an unnamed publisher. Kaneko also said that while the lack of information was frustrating, they were now contractually regulated by the publisher, who had “been supporting the projectâs development up to this point.” While the initial 2022 campaign blew past its initial goal, the team had been open about how little two million goes split between multiple projects, that the money raised was to develop demos to secure more conventional funding. While crowdfunding can help cult developers back on their feet, it more frequently becomes another headache in an already troubled publishing environment. Through the summer, Shibuya Scramble‘s developers have been fighting the crowdfunding platform itself for somehow losing their money. The same statement from Digital Bros reveals they’re also dropping the action RPG The Directorate: Novitiate and a follow-up to 505âs decade old WW2 free-to-play Battle Island. If the wording is accurate, it seems Armed Fantasia will be hanging up its spurs for the foreseeable future. It also leaves the fate of Penny Blood unknown as well, as of the two projects Fantasia appeared much further along, not to mention suffering publisher complications of its own. There's a fight for AI talent that's playing out in the classroom. Sarah Soule, the dean of Stanford's Graduate School of Business, told Business Insider that frontier AI labs — with their enormous computing resources, data, and coming IPOs — are becoming an increasingly powerful draw for professors. "There is an allure for faculty," she said about the trend. "I won't lie, I worry about this." The pull is already evident at Stanford. Andrew Hall and Chad Jones, two GSB professors, are both on leave this year. And Stanford University isn't alone. Soule had just gotten off a public panel with Aaron Chatterji, OpenAI's chief economist, who is on leave from Duke University. Stanford lets its tenured faculty take two years of unpaid leave to join the private sector every seven years. Faculty can take longer leaves for government service, as the school's former provost, Condoleezza Rice, did to become the Secretary of State. Professors often come back to the school, the University told Business Insider. Westley Hartmann, who has taught at Stanford since 2003, took seven months of unpaid leave to work for Amazon. Still, the trend comes as AI labs continue to substantially strengthen their recruiting hand. Leading AI labs continue to amass capital, computing power, and market influence. Working inside one can offer researchers a chance to shape a technology with enormous economic and social consequences — and, potentially, share in its financial upside. Stanford said it does not view faculty collaborations or industry leaves as zero-sum losses. The university described them as part of a broader ecosystem that can help professors stay close to technological development and bring those experiences back into their research, teaching, and work with students. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    "There's no question that the opportunity to work with frontier AI labs is attractive to faculty," Kristin Harlan, the head of dean's communications for Stanford's GSB, said. "We see those relationships as complementary to Stanford's academic mission, not separate from it." Soule said academia still offers something the labs cannot: freedom to pursue long-term research without the same pressure for immediate results. "I suspect that the freedom to do what you want to do and to take a very long time to do it will be possibly something that won't be the case at the frontier labs," she said. AI is also adding a budget problem for schools. Stanford University entered into an enterprise agreement with Anthropic over the summer, Soule said, giving students, faculty, and staff access to Claude's suite of tools. Stanford also has shared computing resources, cloud capacity, and hardware investments for research. Researchers doing the most advanced AI work often need far more than a chatbot subscription, and providing enough computing power is getting increasingly expensive. Soule said Stanford's AI-related research costs are rising, while future spending is "super hard to forecast." Frontier labs, meanwhile, can offer the enormous compute and data resources that university leaders are struggling to match. "I don't have a good answer for it," she said about the increasing budgets. "Probably, most deans and most college presidents are really worried about this issue, because it's really daunting to think about." No comments right now, check back later. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Xavier Sztejnberg, a finance professor at the McCombs School of Business at the University of Texas Austin, who previously worked in M&A. He founded the Wall Street for McCombs Leadership Program in 2016. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. When I started Wall Street for McCombs a decade ago, we sent fewer than 10 UT students to New York for investment banking. UT Austin was a powerhouse in Houston, but we realized we needed a major presence in New York to become a powerhouse school in finance generally. For the summer of 2027, we've helped around 150 students land internships at more than 50 banks, and we've focused on growing our market share at the very top firms. There's a very rigorous admissions process for my program now that interest has swelled. Students apply during their sophomore year, and we usually get almost 500 applications for only 75 spots. Applicants draft resumes, write essays, and go through two rounds of behavioral and technical interviews, the first with student leaders in the group and the second with me. The students who do get in focus on three things: formal training, one-on-one coaching, and mentorship from the alumni board. I view Wall Street for McCombs as a leadership program, not an internship training club. When we identify students, we look for the ones who will become successful alumni and give back to UT. Interviews for junior summer internships are happening earlier and earlier, starting now in November of sophomore year. The timeline can be penalizing for later bloomers, but we've just had to adapt to the reality of the marketplace and have shifted our admissions timeline from October to September. The freshman-year investment banking clubs are helpful, since they train students who eventually enter my program and sit for early interviews. Landing the internship is only half the battle — the other half is getting the return offer, so we spend a lot of time coaching kids to succeed at their summer jobs. We really focus on the fundamentals and technical skills, which are still important on the job, even with AI. They still have to understand the concepts of building a model, since they can't sit in a board meeting and open ChatGPT. We run a banking simulation during the course, where students create a pitchbook for a real corporate client, like Nike or Pepsi. The project trains them to work in a team and with a client, and getting practice with the grunt work helps them hit the ground running at their summer internships. The winning teams present to the client, usually to the company's CFO. The alumni base is incredibly engaged, and they make it a mission to hire more Longhorns. Alumni take ownership of a student every year, coaching them through the process, and ultimately try to grow the UT presence at their firms. Unfortunately, it's a changing world, and a lot of schools are mimicking our model, so we've had to step up our game to make sure UT students still excel. The secret sauce is in the execution and finesse. We have a nearly 100% return-offer rate, and placement is a big part of why. We've built strong relationships with the firms, and I know where students will thrive. Investment banks are like people, with different personalities and needs. It's about optimizing for cultural fit. Beyond being well-prepared, UT students are uniquely humble. They're very collaborative, and the banks love that — I've even seen groups of students preparing for the same interview together. My program has become a positive feedback loop: the more students we place in New York, the more people want to come to UT, which makes the student body even stronger and helps us place more people. Plenty of excellent wireless car chargers can charge your phone on the go while also serving as a mount. I usually recommend these for everyday use, especially since the latest generation of wireless car chargers is Qi2 magnetic, so you don't even need a clamp to mount your phone. For long-haul journeys, I recommend wired car chargers instead because they support much faster charging speeds and let you recharge several devices at once. If you're traveling with a laptop or a Chromebook, your car charger needs to support at least 60W to 65W minimum to be compatible. That's not enough power to be split between two devices, though, which is where the best 100W car chargers come in. I have used countless car chargers through the years. Anker, Baseus, and UGREEN are the top 3 most reliable brands for charging tech, so it's no surprise that, based on my hands-on testing, the best 100W car chargers are from these brands.      Anker's tri-ported marvel is surprisingly affordable for the power and number of ports it delivers. The Anker Nano Car Charger (167.5W, 3 Ports) has one USB-A and two USB-C ports and has a combined 167.5W power rating. This compact charger supports both Samsung and Apple fast-charging profiles. The first USB-C port supports 100W, while the second USB-C port is rated 45W. Lastly, the USB-A port supports up to 22.5W. Anker's proprietary smart chip regulates the voltage and temperature, making it both efficient and safe. Anker includes a 3.3ft USB-C to USB-C cable and offers an 18-month warranty. While the Anker Nano Car Charger usually costs $53.99, it goes on sale very frequently. In fact, it's only $37.79 on Amazon as of this writing. It has two built-in, 105W, 31.5-inch retractable USB-C cables coming out the top, and one 33W USB-C and one 30W USB-A port in the base. There are now three apps that will deliver from Costco to your door. When it comes to price, though, there's a difference. DoorDash and Uber Eats expanded their partnerships with Costco last week. DoorDash said it now delivers from Costco stores around the US, while Uber Eats now offers delivery from the chain in 47 states, up from its previous 17. These complement Costco's existing partnership with Instacart, CEO Ron Vachris said on the company's latest earnings call on Thursday. Instacart has delivered from Costco stores since 2017. Costco customers ordering via DoorDash and Uber Eats tend to be "significantly younger than our overall member base," Vachris said. Delivery customers use the option when they need a few items while still regularly visiting a Costco store, he added. But are each of the three delivery services comparably priced? And how much of a premium are customers paying over going to the store? To find out, I checked the cost of 15 items at a Costco store near me in Washington, DC. Then, I compared the total to the cost of ordering those same items through Instacart, Uber Eats, and DoorDash. Here's what I found. The 15 items I chose span the grocery categories at Costco, from Kirkland Signature Paper Towels to prime ribeye steaks. I also threw in a few items long popular with Costco shoppers, such as a rotisserie chicken and butter croissants. To make the comparison with the apps fair, I made sure to order from the same store that I visited — and on the same day that I visited. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    I also added my Costco membership to each of the apps. Uber Eats and DoorDash required this, while Instacart lets users order from Costco without a membership, though they might pay more. I did not use any of the paid memberships that the apps offer, such as Uber One, though shoppers who use those might save more. Here's how much the items alone cost without tax, fees, a tip, or discounts: Costco in-store: $300.83 Uber Eats: $336.75 DoorDash: $337.64 Instacart: $380.65 Every item on my list cost more through the apps than it did at the store. And while the prices on Uber Eats and DoorDash were usually close to each other, those on Instacart tended to be the highest. Each app applied a consistent markup. Uber Eats charged about 12% more than store prices, while DoorDash was closer to 11%. On Instacart, prices were 24% higher. An Instacart spokesperson said that retailers like Costco set item prices on Instacart. A DoorDash spokesperson said that the pricing structure varies between retailers on the app. Initially, my list included two alcohol items: A 1.75-liter bottle of Kirkland Signature French Vodka and a 750-milliliter bottle of Veuve Clicquot Brut Champagne, both of which I saw were in stock at the store that I visited. I cut these two items because I couldn't find them on Uber Eats or DoorDash. An Uber spokesperson said that the company plans to launch alcohol delivery with Costco, but did not provide a timeline. A DoorDash spokesperson also declined to confirm when the service would start delivering booze. The cost of delivery increased when I reached the checkout page. Here's how much my 15 products were with everything, including sales tax as well as fees, discounts, and a 5% tip that the apps applied: Costco in-store: $318.88 Uber Eats: $373.20 DoorDash: $328.27 Instacart: $419.36 DoorDash was the cheapest delivery option, thanks largely to a $50 discount that the service is offering on Costco orders until November. Otherwise, the cost would be $378.27 all in.  Paying about $10 — about 3% — more than store prices to have everything delivered seems like a reasonable deal. The long-term question, though, is whether paying closer to 20% more will be worth it when the discount presumably goes away. Instacart remained the most expensive option, with the total cost about 32% higher than shopping in-store. Whether the higher costs are worth it depends on your needs. Instacart customers have told me over the years that they appreciate not having to lug huge packs of paper goods up stairs. Many shoppers, especially in big cities, don't have cars, which makes it less practical to haul stuff home from Costco's stores, which are often in suburban neighborhoods. For others, the value of having Costco items delivered might be what CEO Vachris mentioned on this week's earnings call: Getting those few things that you forgot to buy or ran out of since your last Costco run. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Garett Senez, the 39-year-old founder and CEO of Quark Baby. He lives in Vancouver. It's been edited for length and clarity. We make baby-feeding tech and accessories. We started in 2021 with six SKUs. Now we've got 45. A lot of them are made in China. We've got a network there, our factories are there, our molds are there, our lines are there. The tariffs were a huge shock for us. The most immediate thing was: where we can, let's resource out. We took a look at all the other countries where you can produce, like Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Korea. We ended up resourcing a lot of our production to Korea. They have a very high-quality manufacturing base. There are a lot of free-trade agreements that were set. It was expensive. You can move your molds, because a mold is just a metal press. But it's not just the mold that you own. There's a secret sauce of doing things at scale on a production line that you learn over time. You can't just learn that right away. I'd estimate that, with molds and cost of production, it cost us just under $1 million. We're a Canadian company, thank god. The Canadian government has lots of safeguards and things that will help small businesses in times of trouble. We're able to leverage the government a lot, but it absolutely hit the bottom line. It was a gut punch because we had large purchase orders that we had to say no to because that SKU became unbuyable. There were products that were out of stock because I could not bring them in when shipping was so expensive. It's the uncertainty of not knowing, if I bring something in, am I going to make margin? If I order a certain quantity, am I going to be able to ship it? Those things get really complicated, really quickly. As of now, I've found ways around most of those opportunities. Our business is great now, and we're back on a steady track. From a Canadian perspective — and we're still a Canadian holding company — we asked: what does our transfer pricing look like? We're going to ship stuff from Korea to the US; can we move that up to Canada? We have four warehouses, and we move stuff between Canada and the United States all the time. They canceled the $800 minimum, where we could ship our Canadian goods to the United States without having to file. Our entire drop-shipping business to the United States stopped, and we had to find a new warehouse in the US. There's now a tariff block between my warehouses. There are still stranded goods, and I'm on my third drop-shipper. All in, it's probably hit my business to the tune of $2 million, including IP, resourcing, and lost sales. That's probably 90% from the tariff on China and 10% from the tariff on Canada. Baby goods were among the preferred goods they didn't target; if I were in aluminum or cars, it'd probably be different. If Canada doesn't get an agreement with the United States, I may relocate to the US. I'm trying not to. I'm here, and our employees are here. But, from an operational perspective, it may not make sense to be in Canada longterm. 90% of our business is in the US. Cross-border doesn't make sense; it's just too tough. It's mind-boggling how this relationship has frayed. There's a galvanizing action that Canada's had: "Let's band together, elbows up." I do believe that there's a localized movement that will help buoy our business. Do I think it will make a long-run difference? No. As a small business, you're a small sailboat in a big ocean being tossed around. That's how it feels. It feels like I've lost a lot of control. That said, the baby industry is very small, everybody knows each other, and there's been a really good sharing of resources. There's been good sharing of resources from an industry perspective, but from a tariff perspective, it's been so hard. I put my baby on a billboard. This is my life. Sometimes you just can't find capital; I wrote another $300,000 check in April this year just to keep this business going. So yeah, it's been emotionally tough. I've seen 30% of the businesses I know in this industry already die. That's very sobering, but it's also galvanizing toward action. Particularly in entrepreneurship, the ones who refuse to quit are the ones who actually last. So we're just fighting all the time. We are always, always innovating. We had a really cool product in 2022 that was called out on Twitter by Elon Musk. The next year, everyone has their knockoff of our product. Well, you have to innovate. That's what keeps you above water. It's the fun part. You're in a boxing match. You're sticking and moving. How do I keep my head above water? That's it. Continuously innovative, doing things better, and then winning. Tough times don't last, but tough people do. The business environment will always be competitive, but the nuances and externalities will change. Change with them. Try to find a way to keep yourself motivated, even when it's dark. It was the day after the Fall Equinox, and we were partying on a rooftop, pulling tarot cards about our love lives. The location might surprise you: a venture capital firm's office overlooking the Manhattan skyline. Wait, what's astrology got to do with venture capital? We were at a launch party for a social-astrology app called Lora. The party was hosted by Lora founder Michelle Parsons at the offices of her pre-seed backer — AlleyCorp — in SoHo. Astrology is a hot subject in tech. Co-Star, a leading social app for the star-inclined, was acquired by AI company Midjourney this summer, casting a spotlight on the space. Investors and the astrology-obsessed alike want to know: Will an AI-era app take the crown as the next big app in the sector? "This is a space I've been thinking about for a long time," said Luc Ryan-Schreiber, an investor at AlleyCorp who spearheads the firm's incubation projects — including Lora. "With AI, there was an opportunity to do something a little bit more interactive." Lora, for instance, lets users interact with an AI-powered chatbot that offers advice on personal development, relationships — pretty much anything you want — based on your astrological birth chart. While there is a litany of other astrology apps ready for download, perhaps the biggest competitors in the market are the larger LLM models themselves. Anyone can upload their star chart to ChatGPT or Claude, and then spend hours on end prompting the machine to spit out answers. Lora's founder, Parsons, said she didn't want to put out another app that gives people the answers they want to hear. Instead of "sycophantic" responses from an AI bot or a straightforward daily horoscope, Parsons wants Lora to help people recognize "patterns" in their lives, whether in relationships or in private. As two single women living in New York City, naturally, we had questions about our love lives. The biggest lesson we both took home from Benveniste: Pain is the price of love. On the elevator journey to the roof, we got cozy with fellow Lora party attendees. Not a word was spoken until someone broke the silence by asking everyone for their Big Three. (That's your sun, moon, and rising sign.) Walking into the party, we were met with a manifestation board where guests wrote down their prayers for prosperity, love, and money. $50K monthly recurring revenue; that someone special, also $100K; no seasonal depression. A DJ was blasting house music, and an open bar with astrology-themed cocktails was grab-and-go ready. Meanwhile, people in tech got busy talking about the stars. "When I was a VC, I'd ask founders what their star sign was," said VC-turned-founder Zehra Naqvi. (She's a Pisces.) She was one of several startup founders in attendance at Lora's launch party. We asked Eric Phillips Waldstein, founder of dating app Beyond, what brought him to the rooftop shindig. "Michelle, but you know, more broadly, the universe," said Waldstein (a Sagittarius). Lora's Parsons is an advisor for his company. He added that the vibes were certainly "better" than a typical VC party. We chatted with attendees about topics including other astrology tools they've tried, AI, the state of dating apps, socializing IRL, and the brisk end of summer. In line for a tarot reading, Mia Cooper, an attendee who works in tech (and is a Pisces), is considering a career change and hoping to get some clarifying answers at Lora's party. Tech > Services & Software Cory Doctorow and the Norwegian Consumer Council are behind a hilarious and insightful ad campaign about how everything's getting worse. September 26, 2026, 1:47 pm ET Imagine, if you will, a pale figure of Death, dressed in a black robe holding a scythe, alongside a handsome, lumberjack-looking Nordic fella who goes by the name Enshittificator. As partners in crime, they conspire to make your life suck, all because they have the power to make digital products and services worse.  If that piques your interest — and maybe sounds too much like real life — a new “anti-enshittification” ad campaign is worth a few minutes of your time. The term “enshittification” was popularized in 2022 by author and activist Cory Doctorow, and its massive cultural surge earned it a place in Merriam-Webster’s slang hub last year. Enshittification is a deliberate process, designed by companies to maximize profit.  More from CNET It starts with luring you to a product or service, then making it so good that you become completely dependent on it. The next step is to pull the rug out from under you by hiding basic features behind a paywall, reducing overall quality and squeezing you for every last dime while providing as little value as possible.  The Death and Enshittificator video above, released on YouTube in mid-September, is the second of a series from the Norwegian Consumer Council, an independent, government-funded nonprofit that advocates for consumer rights. The main character, the Enshittificator, is a bearded Nordic man who says in the first video, released in February, that his “job is to make things shitty.”  The initial video concludes with Mr. Enshittificator getting into a car accident because he didn’t pay a subscription for his braking system, a scenario he appeared to find amusing. In the second video, he meets Death in the hospital, and the two enter into a business relationship. (He now dons a yellow hazmat suit to stay alive.)  The duo spends time making every conceivable product worse, from TVs and toothbrushes to smartphone storage. They point out that products with long lifespans, like the famously indestructible Nokia 3310 — which makes a cameo appearance — only generate revenue once. If companies want a profitable business model, however, they have to use low-quality materials, ensure products can’t be fixed and stop issuing updates.  “Look at all the companies that used to make solid products,” the Enshittificator said. “Where are they now?” “Dead,” Death said, and they share a knowing smile.  The Norwegian Consumer Council’s ads are part of its Breaking Free initiative, a multipronged policy approach to make technology work in favor of consumers, rather than against them. The campaign craftily relies on dark humor to detail how enshittification affects everyday life, from paid subscription models to planned obsolescence, which forces you to buy newer devices.  The videos are also a strikingly accurate commentary on the dismal state of products and gadgets in the digital age. Prices go up while reliability plummets. Companies rely on shady advertising tactics and dodge consumer protection rights.  Doctorow himself collaborated with the nonprofit to help launch the series, which he’s immensely pleased with. In an email to CNET, he said, “The idea that firms’ market power means that they can worsen their offerings with impunity, combined with the minor license to vulgarity of my dirty little word, have proven a winning combination for helping people direct their anger in the right direction.” The enshittification process is relatable and real. In 2020, Apple agreed to pay up to $500 million to settle the landmark “batterygate” class action lawsuit over allegations that it secretly slowed down older iPhone models through software updates. Powerful tech companies have poured massive amounts of money into lobbying against right-to-repair laws, preventing customers from fixing their own devices when they break.   “It’s really important that the products can’t be fixed,” said the Enshittificator. “It breaks, then it dies, so you have to buy a new one. And another one. And another one. And another one. And another one.” “This way, we’re actually slowly killing the planet as well,” a smiling Death said, helpfully chiming in.  The videos also satirize how digital services slowly degrade over time. In one scene, the Enshittificator tells an employee, “The 1,000 pictures of your deceased mother are mine, and you’re going to pay for them.” It’s a direct nod to Google Photos’ 2021 policy shift, which ended free unlimited storage and capped free accounts at 15GB, requiring users to get a subscription to keep already uploaded photos on the platform.  Another scene takes a jab at automakers who sell you basic functionality as an add-on subscription service.  “I don’t have any more money. You have me in the palm of your hand,” said the Enshittificator in a fake presentation about selling cars. “You can crush me. So what do you do? Updates. Radio? Premium feature. Heating? Premium feature. Now I have a shitty car, and I can’t afford a new one, but what I can afford is a small monthly payment!” This is a reference to BMW’s controversial microtransaction model, where it tried to make heated seats and other in-car features part of a subscription plan. While intense consumer backlash forced the German automaker to walk back some of the “add-ons,” several features remain behind a paywall. Other brands have followed suit — Hyundai’s BlueLink and Kia Connect require paid plans to use remote start. For a period, both manufacturers even omitted the remote-start button from the physical key fob, completely blocking owners from using the feature for free. It’s important, though a little depressing, to imagine how much better life would be if companies actually invested money into making their products better, safer and longer-lasting — and not just more profitable for them.  In its Breaking Free: Pathways to a Fair Technological Future report, the Norwegian Consumer Council argues that major tech business models “are often fundamentally incompatible with consumer and human rights.” To dismantle the “walled gardens run by Big Tech feudalists” and end dependence on Big Tech, the nonprofit is pushing for policy reforms built around a three-pronged strategy based on democratic values and principles of openness.  The first is interoperability, which would force platforms to interface with one another. This is already taking shape under the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required Apple to allow third-party app stores and mandated Meta to support external chats in WhatsApp,  Next comes portability, which would allow users to move their contacts, content, photos and anything else to rival services. A subscriber fed up with Spotify adding AI features, for instance, would be able to switch to YouTube Music or Apple Music without losing their saved playlists, thereby eliminating platform lock-in.  Finally, and arguably the most difficult to implement, is decentralization of social media, which could shift social media away from single-entity corporate control toward open networks like the Fediverse (which powers platforms such as Mastodon). Though still evolving as protocols develop, decentralization enhances interoperability, making cross-network movement frictionless. Reining in Big Tech remains an uphill battle, but in the meantime, the campaign offers a hilarious — and painfully accurate — look at the modern digital hellscape. “The true mark of success for a project like this is when other people pick it up and run with it,” Doctorow said.   		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. In some ways, it feels like the world of work has not caught up with the way life is in 2026. It may stay up to date on the technology, but the culture seems to be way behind the modern reality of trying to find a job.  In almost every industry and especially the corporate ones, job seekers will told that they need to be open to opportunities, build their personal brand, and know where to look online and elsewhere to get to the job openings before everyone else does. That doesn't stop hundreds of people at a time from applying the for the same role, though, and a lot of the time a hiring manager is going to ignore a LinkedIn message begging for a networking 'coffee chat'. A lot of the process feels like a pointless exercise with no job offer at the end of it. The reality is that knowing the right people is more important than ever when it comes to finding work. Studies agree that for recent college graduates in particular, simply having a degree does not necessarily give them much of an edge in the employment market. More people are looking for a job with their qualifications, and they don't necessarily make them stand out. It is no surprise that most people who have spent a long time looking for a job are pretty cynical about the process. There are only so many rejections and straight-up sending applications into the ether that anybody can take. Add to the fact that anyone seeking work is supposed to be permanently switched on and marketing themselves, and you get a phenomenon like the #DESPERATE profile picture on LinkedIn, with job seekers using the label to advertise exactly how they feel about trying to find a role.   Supposedly, things are not necessarily as bad as they seem with the labor market. A survey by Indeed this summer suggested that levels of unemployment were likely to remain steady from this year into the next, with only a 1.6% decrease in job postings between now and June 2027. For anybody who is out of work and struggling, though, even the smallest dip is likely to be noticeable. There remains a lot of uncertainty with how AI is going to continue to affect the workplace, with many forecasters in the survey expecting it to put pressure the wages of the college-educated in particular. As many reacting to the #DESPERATE phenomenon have argued, it is not exactly the greatest marketing to attract potential employers. It is more an expression of frustration about a job market which seems to be a lot more difficult than it needs to be. There are plenty of qualified, competent people who want nothing more than to earn a living, but they have to be given the chance to do that. In the face of so much competition and rejection, it is no wonder that they poke fun at themselves and also the system that they have no choice but to participate in. Want More? Nvidia has always led in desktop GPUs — until now. The RTX 50-Series' disastrous launch was the deciding factor in the GPU war against AMD, and Team Red won despite releasing only three GPUs (with different variants) in the RDNA 4 lineup. This low-key approach worked well for AMD, since the PC community shifted toward budget and mid-range builds instead of chasing top performance because of the high costs. Still, the question lingers: When will AMD return to the flagship models? The last time it made a high-end GPU was in 2022 with the RX 7900 XTX, and it wasn't great. However, this edge over Nvidia and the fact that Team Green's priorities have shifted give AMD a reason to target the premium segment once more, and it might already be doing so, making the GPU that Nvidia skipped out on. The RTX 3060 is back, and it's not for gaming anymore The Blackwell GPUs came out in January 2025 and, more than a year later, are still in short supply. As if the GPUs aren't expensive enough, the RTX 5090 is still being scalped for more than $5,000 in some markets because AI companies love the GPU and are gobbling up demand, leaving scraps for the people the GPU is actually meant for. Nvidia has offered mid-cycle upgrades to the original RTX lineup with the Super GPUs, ironing out flaws and delivering better performance and value overall. The Super GPUs usually launch a year after the base RTX lineup, but Nvidia may not have anything to offer this year despite earlier plans. Rising memory costs and barely meeting demand for the RTX 50-Series GPU are the reasons why plans for the Super refresh are effectively shelved. If this setback isn't enough, Nvidia might have nothing to show for it even in 2027, as numerous reports suggest. This puts the GPU market in a difficult spot, since Nvidia remains the default pick for high-end builds. With RDNA 5 GPUs, AMD is set to return to the flagship market, and it may be coming back with a bang. Reports suggest the lineup will be based on a 3nm architecture, move toward GDDR7 memory, and offer improved specifications. One reliable leaker claims one of the higher-end GPUs in the RDNA 5 lineup will be codenamed AT2, which is supposed to feature 70 CUs, and that the RDNA 5 GPUs overall are targeting 3.1–3.4 GHz (via AnandTech). Based on early specs, the AT2 is estimated to be 15–25% faster than the RX 9070 XT. This roughly puts the AT2 against a supposed RTX 5080 Super, if the GPU ever comes out, but alas. Historically, xx-80 Super GPUs have seen big improvements in price-to-performance because of lower prices and higher performance than the base GPU, which is exactly what's needed right now to make higher-end gaming more feasible given how expensive GPUs are. Fortunately, AMD is compensating for the shortfall left by Nvidia, even if it's with only one GPU. The next Xbox and PlayStation consoles will both use the RDNA architecture, so the AT2 GPU is a taste of what next-generation gaming will look like. AT2 will be the only GPU from the RDNA 5 family to be released next year, and like Nvidia, AMD is also delaying the rest of the releases to 2028. With China's CXMT entering the memory market, supply is increasing, and memory prices are expected to ease by 2028, making that a feasible time to launch the next generation of GPUs. However, AMD isn't willing to wait till 2028 to give everyone a taste of what it's working on. If all goes well, the AT2 will only increase customers' hunger for what the next generation of GPUs holds, especially coming after a 2-year hiatus. Later in 2028, AMD plans to release AT0, the GPU meant to go toe-to-toe with the RTX 6090, suggesting that Nvidia has a long battle ahead. Nvidia's AI focus has led it to neglect the desktop GPU market. Following a poor RTX 50-Series launch and no new GPU for 2 years straight, Nvidia has a lot of expectations to fulfill with the upcoming RTX 60-Series GPUs. This gives AMD plenty of time to catch up, and aside from a return to the higher-end GPU sector, it's also working on a new Neural Rendering model akin to DLSS  (via AnandTech) With this gap, we may reach a point where Nvidia no longer has an edge over AMD, either in terms of feature set or hardware. In any case, all eyes are on the AT2 GPU, meant to fill the gap left by the lack of GPU releases, to see how well it performs. Nevertheless, both Nvidia and AMD will have to surprise their customers. GnuVPN’s mobile app. Promotional image supplied by the company. For years, consumer VPNs were easy to explain: choose a server, create an encrypted tunnel, and route your traffic through it. The product category was built around a fairly simple idea, and the buying criteria followed the same logic, speed, server count, and price. That description is becoming less complete. The way people connect to the internet is now far more fragmented than it was when VPNs first became mainstream consumer software. A laptop may spend the morning on home Wi-Fi, the afternoon on a corporate network, and the evening tethered to a phone. A smartphone can move between Wi-Fi and cellular data repeatedly without the user thinking about it. Travel adds hotel networks, airports, roaming, and increasingly eSIMs. The network keeps changing. The expectation that connectivity should remain private, usable, and largely invisible does not. This changes what users need from a VPN. Encryption still matters, but the practical question is no longer simply whether a tunnel can be created. It is whether that connection remains usable when the network around it changes. That helps explain why protocol choice, once something largely left to technically minded users, is becoming more relevant. WireGuard has become a popular option partly because of its deliberately lean design and focus on performance. But different protocols can respond differently to network conditions, leaving room for alternatives when the obvious choice is not the most practical one. The point is not that users should spend their day manually comparing protocols. Ideally, they should not have to think about them at all. Giving the software more than one way to establish a protected connection simply gives it more room to adapt. GnuVPN is a useful example of that approach. The service supports several connection options, including WireGuard, OpenVPN, SoftEther, and AmneziaWG. WireGuard can serve as an everyday option, while the alternatives provide other ways to establish a connection when network conditions become less straightforward. The same principle applies beyond protocols. A service intended to sit quietly in the background of everyday internet use also needs to work across the devices people actually use. GnuVPN’s downloads page currently offers clients for Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Ubuntu, and Debian. Android distribution also extends beyond Google Play to Huawei AppGallery and Xiaomi GetApps. That breadth matters less as a box-ticking exercise than as a reflection of how fragmented personal computing has become: one person may work on Windows, travel with an Android phone, and keep another machine on Linux. Cross-platform support is therefore part of the same connectivity problem. The tool needs to remain available as the user moves between devices, not just networks. The more interesting shift starts one step earlier. A traditional VPN assumes the user is already online. It protects a connection that already exists. An eSIM solves a different problem: getting the device onto a mobile network in the first place. Technically, those are separate jobs. To someone landing in another country, the distinction matters much less. The immediate task is simply to get online without unnecessary roaming friction and then use that connection with privacy in mind. That is why the growing overlap between VPNs and travel connectivity is worth watching. GnuVPN now offers eSIMSecure plans that combine mobile data with a VPN subscription, placing access and privacy in the same product flow rather than treating them as completely separate purchases. The broader mobile market helps explain why that combination is becoming more plausible. According to the GSMA Intelligence 2025 Global Consumer Survey, 12% of consumers who had travelled internationally during the previous 12 months used an eSIM while abroad. More than 70% of those users obtained a travel eSIM from a mobile operator. This does not mean every VPN will become an eSIM provider, or that the two products are interchangeable. It points to something simpler: the line between tools that provide connectivity and tools that protect it is becoming less rigid. For VPN companies, that changes the competitive picture. Server count and benchmark speed still matter, but so do continuity across devices, resilience across different network environments, and ease of everyday use. None of this means a VPN is becoming an all-purpose connectivity tool. It cannot repair a poor mobile signal, guarantee access through every restrictive network, replace endpoint security, or prevent a website from recognizing a signed-in user. More protocols do not remove those limits, and adding an eSIM does not make mobile connectivity itself a privacy technology. What is changing is how much of the surrounding experience a VPN is expected to handle. The original consumer VPN flow was deliberately visible: open the app, choose a country, press Connect. Increasingly, the expectation is that the service should simply keep working as the user moves between devices and network environments, with fewer reasons to think about what is happening underneath. Taken together, protocol flexibility, broad platform support, and travel connectivity point to a wider shift in the category. They are increasingly being treated as parts of the same product experience rather than separate technical features. That may be a more useful way to think about where VPNs are heading. The next stage is likely to be less about adding another headline feature and more about making protected connectivity fit more naturally into the way people already get online. A year ago, Meta was struggling to convince Silicon Valley that it could keep up in the AI race. Now it has one of the industry's hottest products. Muse, Meta's new personal AI assistant, has rocketed to the top of the App Store and become a victory lap for CEO Mark Zuckerberg's massive AI spending. Meta's Connect conference this week was all about the app, which AI chief Alexandr Wang — who is 29 and has been posting risqué memes of Muse's mascot all week — called a "banger." Getting there required months of painstaking work, a team led by former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and thousands of employees pulled from across Meta to teach the agent how to actually get things done, employees told Business Insider. Meta also snapped up top AI agent talent through acqui-hires, including the leaders of Dreamer, an AI agent startup. Whether Meta can sustain Muse's momentum is another question. Competitors like Instinct are thriving, and OpenAI is widely expected to launch a rival. Privacy concerns have also arisen, as Muse requires broad access to users' accounts to function. Meta employees are still reeling from a year of mass layoffs, employee surveillance, and low morale. For now, at least, Muse's success — and a more than 20% increase in Meta's stock price since its launch — has become a morale boost, employees said. It also proves that Meta remains firmly in the AI race after being seen as a laggard a year ago. "Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said. Muse's success was far from inevitable. Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team, has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch." Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests. Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added. Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort. That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it. The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before. "Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect. Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor. Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies." He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel. When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch. He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent. While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said. Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted. Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team. Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X. The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta, Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before. Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator, Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant. Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction. "We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note. Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes. "They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said. At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote. Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath. For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse. "The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X. Have a tip? Explore ↓ Network ↓  By Jerome London    Updated 21 hours ago, September 26, 2026   While paid dating apps bleed subscribers, a free service tucked inside Facebook has quietly become one of the biggest players in the market — and its own product manager thinks she knows why. Meta says the free app now has 21 million users, and the paid services people used to pay for are shrinking around it. Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, reported 13.3 million paying users in the second quarter of 2026, down 6% from a year earlier. Bumble’s paying users fell 21.1% to 3.2 million, and in August it dropped its founding rule and started letting men message first. The dating-app market posted its first annual revenue decline in 2025, to about $6 billion. “I think people are just fed up with their core human desire of finding connection and finding love being monetized,” Facebook Dating product manager Neha Kumar told WIRED, which reported the 21 million figure in December 2025. In the U.S., 1.77 million people aged 18 to 29 use it daily. One user, Ethan Sanders, 32, said the tone is different: “I’ve come across profiles saying things like, ‘I’m not here for games.'” The fatigue is measurable. In a 2024 Forbes Health survey, 78% of recent app users said they felt burned out, and a Kinsey Institute survey found only 22% of Gen Z and millennials use apps as their main way to date. Bumble founder Whitney Wolfe Herd told staff in 2025: “Dating apps are feeling like a thing of the past.” People didn’t stop looking. On Sept. 23 and 24, a Threads post asking “Can we get single people no kids thread going 👀” drew more than 30,000 replies and 6.9 million views, with singles answering in dating-profile format: age, “no kids,” job, city, photo. One read, “38. No Kids. Single. RN. LA📍” The same day, a 56-year-old man’s post drew nearly 8,000 likes: “We met on Facebook dating 3 years after my divorce and life has been great! She’s 54 yrs and I’m 56 yrs. Divorce is never the end, there is plenty of life still to live.” “No kids” now leads the profile. A 2024 Pew Research Center report found the share of U.S. adults under 50 without children who say they’re unlikely to ever have kids rose from 37% in 2018 to 47% in 2023, and 57% of them said a major reason is that they just don’t want to. Meeting online was already the most common path: Stanford’s How Couples Meet and Stay Together survey found the share of heterosexual couples who met online rose from 2% in 1995 to 39% in 2017, overtaking meeting through friends around 2013. By          David Cox                        Mark Shaheel Lal is the founder of Living Positive Fiji and a reconciliation officer for the Fiji Truth and Reconciliation Commission. He says: "The majority of my friends, they got HIV through crystal meth." He was photographed at the AIDS conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in July.                                                           Ian Cheibub for NPR                                       hide caption  Best known as a tropical paradise and honeymoon destination, the island nation of Fiji now has the unfortunate distinction of facing two intertwined epidemics: HIV and addiction to crystal meth. With HIV cases rising by 12-fold between 2010 and 2025, in mid-September, Fiji's government declared a national emergency. Estimates are that there are upward of 9,000 cases; the country's health minister has announced that 1 in 60 adults are now living with HIV. At the July AIDS 2026 conference in Rio, Jason Mitchell, a public health specialist leading Fiji's HIV response, described it as the fastest-growing HIV epidemic in the world, noting that two-thirds of cases are in those ages 20-34. "Our young, active, productive population is currently being infected with HIV, and unless we find solutions quickly, this will continue to get worse," he says. A key cause is another parallel epidemic — the rampant use of crystal meth among the nation's youth, who often inject it. That has led to transmission through shared needles. "Two of my best friends passed away," says Mark Lal, a 25-year-old HIV activist from Fiji's capital of Suva. "The majority of my friends, they got HIV through crystal meth." Crystal meth has long been available to some degree within Fiji — the islands are a known transit hub for the drug between South America and the eventual destinations of Australia and New Zealand. But since COVID, meth use has soared, something Fiji's HIV experts attribute to the lethal combination of rising unemployment and ever more accessible drugs. "COVID was a difficult time for Fijians," says Sailosi Soqo, a doctor working on the national HIV response team. "Most lost their jobs, got less hours or were stuck at home. At the same time, we suspect that the travel restrictions, along with increased border security, decreased the movement of narcotics onto their target countries. Drugs that would otherwise have moved on stayed in Fiji, seeding this domestic market which didn't really exist before." Soqo suggests that spiraling unemployment, combined with worsening mental health due to the impacts of lockdown, led to more young Fijians turning to meth, even preteens. "The communities I work with report children as young as 9 using injectable drugs," he says. According to Dashika Balak, a doctor who leads Fiji's national HIV treatment, care and support efforts, the risk of HIV transmission has also been exacerbated by a nationwide shift from smoking meth to injecting it. This includes the so-called "bluetoothing" or "hotspotting" practice where one person injects the drug and then another person injects their blood. Bluetoothing is known to occur in settings of extreme poverty as a cheaper way of getting high. But Mitchell believes that its popularity in Fiji is partially because sharing all manner of things is a part of national culture — both alcohol and the ceremonial drink kava are consumed via a communal glass or bowl — and partially due to a scarcity of needles. Soqo says that law enforcement in Fiji has cracked down on needle availability in an attempt to curb meth use, something that he believes has inadvertently encouraged bluetoothing. Unfortunately, bluetoothing has fueled the spread of HIV. Reports suggest that on average, one infected person in Fiji will pass the virus on to 10 others. "You add the existing culture in Fiji of sharing things, plus the limited access to clean injecting equipment, and you get the perfect storm for HIV transmission," says Soqo. Fiji's HIV epidemic is also spreading in other ways, including risky sexual practices. "What we do know is that sexual intercourse, as a transmission route, made up roughly 50% of the new HIV cases for 2025," says Soqo. Balak says that low condom use is encouraging the spread of HIV. A 2021 survey found that among 15- to 49-year-olds with multiple sexual partners in the past year, only 24% of men and 9% of women used a condom the last time they had sex. Lal can attest to this — having contracted HIV himself in the summer of 2024 through unprotected sex with a male partner. "You let your guard down once, and boom, it happens," he says. The surge in cases has led to an influx of foreign aid to support new HIV testing, prevention and treatment programs. Concerned about rising rates of infections and the potential for the epidemic to spread more widely through the Pacific, the Australian government announced a new $48 million funding package in August. According to a statement to NPR, the government is committed to supporting Fiji's HIV response to prevent new infections, improve early diagnosis and expand access to treatment. One of the first priorities for Australian organizations working with Fiji is to make HIV testing available at all antenatal clinics. In 2025, 59 babies were born with HIV. "We're trying to get a reliable rollout of these tests so that every single pregnant woman anywhere in the country will be tested for HIV," says Storm Holwill, a public health physician working at Melbourne's Peter Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity. Anyone who is HIV positive would then be placed on viral-suppressing medications known as antiretrovirals to limit the chances of HIV being passed on in utero. Blocking new infections on a wider scale is far more challenging. Meth use is most prevalent in some of Fiji's poorest and most vulnerable populations, many of whom have no fixed address. This makes it difficult for medical professionals to test and prescribe treatments. Balak explains that while anywhere between 9,100 and 12,000 people in Fiji are thought to have HIV, only 5,676 of these cases have been officially diagnosed. Even fewer are regularly taking antiretrovirals to keep their condition under control. "Some stop treatment, and some cannot be reached because their contact details are incomplete," she says. This means that while Australia's aid is providing Fiji with plentiful access to medications such as PrEP pills to block HIV infections, getting these drugs to the right people is not straightforward.                  Dr. Jason Mitchell is the head of Fiji's National HIV Outbreak and Cluster Response Taskforce.                                                           Ian Cheibub for NPR                                       hide caption  "We've just introduced PrEP about two months back," says Mitchell. "The uptake has been very slow, while at the same time, antiretroviral treatment is also freely available, but it's currently sitting on shelves." Lal argues that one of the biggest problems is a lack of awareness. He says many people in Fiji have never heard of these medications. Even for those who have, obtaining them requires a lengthy journey to one of three dedicated clinical centers, either in the cities of Suva and Lautoka or the town of Labasa. With Fiji's population spread across more than 100 islands, Lal says that such a journey likely deters many people from seeking care. "If they know the medications are far away, they won't even want to access them," he says. "In a country like ours where religion is big, people would — rather than go — pray and believe that God will heal them." To improve access to PrEP and antiretrovirals, Balak and her colleagues have started creating dedicated HIV response teams in 21 locations across the country. "They will soon be able to order their own antiretrovirals [and] dispense and fully manage their patients on their own," she says. To track down more people living with HIV, the team is also recruiting and training peer support workers — including some existing meth users who are HIV positive. Balak says she hopes that this could be a way to connect more of the people at most risk of contracting HIV with medical teams. Methamphetamine use remains a tense issue, and some of the proposed schemes to address the spread of HIV have clashed with law enforcement. To break the chains of infections stemming from contaminated needles, Soqo has proposed supplying thousands of sterile needles and syringes to communities of methamphetamine users. However, Soqo says the government is blocking the plan. "The director prosecutor has told us, 'If you hand these out, we'll arrest you, and we'll charge you for aiding and abetting,'" he says. "As a result, I now have a warehouse full of needles and syringes, just collecting dust." Fiji's government did not respond to a request for comment from NPR. However, there is more optimism that other approaches could make a significant difference. Fiji is set to receive supplies of the drug lenacapavir, an injectable form of PrEP that provides those at risk of infection due to sexual behavior or drug use near 100% protection from HIV. Because this new preventive drug only needs to be administered twice yearly, Mitchell believes it will be easier to convince people to use it compared with daily pills. To prevent women from contracting HIV from their partners while pregnant, antenatal clinics hope to start offering vaginal rings, which slowly release a protective antiretroviral drug over the course of a month. Such innovations are badly needed. Projections suggest that if the epidemic continues at its current pace, 25,000 people in Fiji will be living with HIV by 2029, figures that Soqo says would push Fiji's fragile health system to the brink of collapse. "Time is not on our side," says Soqo. "With the current numbers, we're already struggling. All our main hospitals are overcrowded and have chronic issues with staffing shortages. Our tuberculosis hospitals and primary healthcare facilities are telling us they're seeing an increase in advanced HIV cases and are overwhelmed. Imagine what things will be like in three years' time. There is an urgent need for more action now." We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Belkin accessories occupy an interesting space in the market, since they are usually good alternatives to official Apple or Samsung products. The brand competes well with official iPhone accessories, especially when it comes to chargers and MagSafe solutions. Still, Belkin's reputation does not mean that every product from the company is automatically the best choice. There has also been a big increase in competition for Belkin now. Brands such as Anker, Ugreen and ESR also offer accessories with similar proposals, often at better prices. Still, Belkin can still differentiate itself in some categories with its build quality, compatibility with Apple devices and practical features meant to make everyday use easier. This becomes clearer with products such as charging docks, power banks, and hubs, where small differences can greatly change the experience. For that reason, among so many options available, we separated some Belkin accessories that offer meaningful advantages over competitors and official accessories, making them more interesting choices depending on what you need. If you have several Apple devices, this Belkin UltraCharge model is one of the best purchases to consider. It can charge an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods at the same time, and it also supports 25W Qi2 with compatible iPhones. The base includes a 45W USB-C adapter, so you don't need another power supply. This speed also translates well in tests. MacWorld considered the UltraCharge Pro the fastest 3-in-1 charger available, recording around 30 to 35 minutes to take an iPhone 16 Pro from 0% to 50%. For comparison, 15W Qi2 chargers usually need approximately 15 minutes more to reach the same charge, giving Belkin's product a good advantage over slower alternatives. Another difference is ChillBoost, an active cooling system that helps control temperature during charging without turning the base into a noisy accessory. For anyone looking for iPhone 17 Pro accessories, this set is hard to beat, especially because the magnetic stand can be adjusted for portrait or landscape use. Its slimmer format is a major advantage. In Vice tests, it took up much less space than the Anker Prime 27,650mAh while still offering enough capacity for notebooks and other devices. That matters because powerful power banks are often inconvenient to carry. The Belkin power bank has a 20,000mAh capacity and can deliver up to 65W through a single USB-C port, enough to top up several compatible laptops. It also has a second USB-C port and a single USB-A port so that you can charge up to three devices at once. Using all three reduces the main port to 45W, with the others sharing the remaining 20W. Belkin also includes a color screen, so it offers more information than power banks that only show battery bars. It displays the remaining charge and the power used on each port, making it easier to see how much each device is actually receiving. This combination also makes it a useful alternative to other Anker accessories for MacBook users. Belkin's Stage Creator Kit stands out because it includes much of the basic equipment you need to record videos with a phone. The box includes an aluminum tripod, a magnetic smartphone mount, and two wireless microphones, which help improve audio quality on an iPhone. Both microphones record in 24-bit/48kHz, have noise reduction and a USB-C receiver for a fast connection. The case gives the microphone up to 36 hours of battery life, and the tripod reaches about 1.7 meters. The magnetic mount also lets you tilt the phone at various angles, making it easier to record without another person. GadgetGuy tested the Stage Creator Kit and rated it as one of the best beginner options in its price range, especially for its user-friendliness. This package is a particularly attractive proposition for beginners, as it costs about the same as the more sophisticated wireless microphone system by itself. For anyone who needs to keep many cables connected to the same device, Belkin's hub is a good option, especially for laptop users. Besides adding more ports, it also works as a stand. The accessory covers many key considerations when choosing a docking station. It offers 11 connections, including two HDMI ports, VGA, USB-C, USB-A, SD and microSD readers, 3.5 mm audio, and 2.5 Gbps Ethernet. It also offers data transfer speeds of up to 10 Gbps and USB-C with power delivery so that you can keep almost everything connected in one place. This combination is great if you use multiple monitors. According to Tom's Guide, this Belkin device supports up to three external displays, while the Anker 675, with a higher suggested price, offers only one HDMI output. The accessory also has an advantage in wired networking, with higher speeds, but it only offers 4K at 60Hz. That doesn't hurt productivity, though it can get in the way for anyone who wants to play at higher refresh rates. If you like taking photos with your phone, Belkin's PowerGrip is also worth a look because it turns your smartphone into a compact camera. The accessory attaches magnetically to the device, adds a larger grip, and includes a physical button for taking photos. The internal 9,300mAh battery also stands out, accompanied by 7.5W wireless charging, an 18W retractable USB-C cable, and the ability to power up to three devices at the same time. Other brands offer a similar concept, such as the ShiftCam SnapGrid Pro, but Belkin has an advantage in battery capacity. The competitor offers only 5,000mAh, although it makes up for that with Qi2 charging and a design that makes switching between portrait and landscape easier. The PowerGrip, on the other hand, focuses much more on versatility, even including a thread for tripods. So, for anyone who needs to take photos or record video regularly, it is a consistent option that combines grip and an extra battery in one accessory. To choose these Belkin accessories, we prioritized products that offered a clear advantage over comparable alternatives, rather than simply selecting the best-rated ones. We considered charging speed, battery capacity, overall capability, portability, and each product's versatility, since each product serves a different purpose. We also used independent reviews and direct comparisons whenever possible. These sources help confirm where a Belkin product actually performed better than a competitor, while also highlighting possible limitations. This detail matters because an accessory can be superior in one area but not be the best option in every aspect. For that reason, the list includes only products with a clear, well-supported advantage.
